question: The on-call engineer is paged several times a night for brief error spikes that fix themselves, and has started ignoring pages. Last week a real outage went unanswered for forty minutes. What should the alerting be based on?
context: Today an alert fires whenever the 5xx rate is above 1% for one minute. The service's SLO is 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days.

options.label: Raise the threshold to 5% so only the larger spikes wake anyone up
options.why: A slow, steady 2% failure rate — which spends a month's error budget in a day and a half — would now never page. The threshold is arbitrary either way, because it is not tied to what users were promised.

options.label: Page on how fast the error budget is burning, over two time windows
options.why: The SLO says how much failure is acceptable; the burn rate says how quickly it is being used. A fast burn over a short window pages at once, a slow burn over hours opens a ticket, and a one-minute blip that barely touches the budget does neither — so a page means something again.

options.label: Only page when the failure lasts for fifteen minutes without a break
options.why: A total outage now goes unanswered for fifteen minutes by design, and a failure that flaps on and off never pages at all. Duration alone ignores how much damage is being done.

options.label: Send every alert to a chat channel and let the team triage by hand
options.why: It removes the noise by removing the page, so the forty-minute outage becomes a message nobody reads at 3 a.m. The problem is which signals page, not whether anything does.
